corrections.new: Imagine being forced to follow state laws, yet being told that this makes you completely free! The Genevan thinker Jean-Jacques Rousseau solved this puzzle with his famous idea of the General Will.
corrections.reason: Rousseau was born in the Republic of Geneva (Genevan), not France, though his writings deeply influenced the French Revolution.

quiz.q: According to Rousseau, what historical development corrupted natural human bliss and turned man into a 'depraved animal'?
options: The emergence of calculating reason and settled society that introduced distinctions of private property.
The innate psychological malice and competitive selfishness inherently present within original human nature.
The total absence of an absolute third-party monarch capable of enforcing formal legal sovereignty.
The failure of early citizens to elect representative assemblies to govern communal affairs.
quiz.why: Rousseau argued that humans were peaceful noble savages until settled civilization and calculating rationality taught greed, inequality, and 'mine and thine'.

quiz.q: How does Rousseau define the General Will that forms the foundation of legitimate political society?
options: The majority consensus formed by tallying citizens' selfish, profit-maximizing actual desires.
The collective sum of the selfless, essentially good real wills of all citizens.
The sovereign decree handed down by an enlightened monarch acting as a third-party beneficiary.
The negotiated compromise reached between competing political parties inside an elected parliament.
quiz.why: Rousseau distinguishes between the selfish actual will and the selfless real will, defining the General Will as the sum of all citizens' good real wills.

quiz.q: Why is Rousseau's General Will famously described as 'Hobbes's Leviathan with his head chopped off'?
options: It completely eliminates all state enforcement and replaces sovereign authority with voluntary individual agreements.
It divides sovereign authority into separate branches to prevent any single institution from exercising absolute power.
It possesses absolute coercive authority like the Leviathan, but diffuses that power throughout the entire community.
It limits the ruler's sovereign power by making them accountable to a periodic bill of fundamental rights.
quiz.why: Both systems grant absolute power to the sovereign, but Rousseau eliminates Hobbes's monarchical ruler and vests supreme authority directly in the people.

quiz.q: In Rousseau's philosophy, how does a citizen achieve 'moral freedom' or positive liberty under the state?
options: By electing competent representatives to debate and enact national legislation on their behalf.
By enjoying a protected private sphere completely free from any governmental interference or taxation.
By retaining the constitutional right to overthrow any government that fails to preserve natural rights.
By directly participating in making the moral laws that they subsequently obey as citizens.
quiz.why: Rousseau equated moral freedom with positive liberty, meaning individuals remain free only when obeying laws they personally deliberated and voted into existence.
